subslides.chapter: by III.18, / F C / ⊥ / D E /, so < F C E ) is a right angle
subslides.symbolic: F center & C contact → / F C / ⊥ / D E / → < F C E ) = ∟
subslides.clause_html:
Since / D E / touches ( A B C ) and / F C / joins center to contact,
/ F C / ⊥ / D E /, so < F C E ) is right.
subslides.just_title: By III.18, the line joined from the center to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent.

subslides.chapter: since < A C E ) is also right, < F C E ) = < A C E ) (less = greater) ⇒⇐
subslides.symbolic: < A C E ) = ∟ → < F C E ) = < A C E ) (part = whole) ⇒⇐
subslides.clause_html:
But < A C E ) is right by construction;
therefore < F C E ) = < A C E ) (the less to the greater) ⇒⇐
subslides.just_title: All right angles are equal (I.post.4), making part < F C E ) equal to whole < A C E ), contradicting I.cn.5.

subslides.chapter: the center of circle ( A B C ) lies on the perpendicular / A C /
subslides.symbolic: ∴ center(( A B C )) ∈ / A C /
subslides.clause_html:
∴ F is not the center, nor any point off / A C /;
the center of ( A B C ) lies on / A C /.
subslides.just_title: The perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact passes through the center of the circle (Q.E.D.).

subslides.symbolic: (1) tangent at C + (3) / C A / ⊥ / D E / ⇒ (2) center ∈ / A C /

/ C A / ⊥ / D E / at contact C ⇒ center ∈ / A C /
Heath observes that III.19 completes the partial converses of III.16 Porism and III.18, and together with III.11–12 proves that two circles touching internally or externally share a common tangent perpendicular to their line of centers.
subslides.just_title: A second partial converse of III.18 also holds: the perpendicular from the center to the tangent passes through the point of contact.
